# Naive Bayes Classifier

::: {.callout-note title="Connection with the theoretical volume"}
The mathematical treatment of conditional probability, Bayes' theorem, and probabilistic classification is developed more deeply in Chapters 3 and 6 of *Mathematical Foundations of Machine Learning* [@rodriguez2026fundamentos].
:::

## Learning objectives

By the end of this chapter, the reader will be able to explain Bayes' theorem in a classification setting, interpret priors, likelihoods, and posteriors, understand the conditional-independence assumption, distinguish categorical and Gaussian Naive Bayes, and evaluate the classifier with held-out data.

## Bayes' theorem

For a class $C$ and observed features $X$,

$$
P(C\mid X)=\frac{P(X\mid C)P(C)}{P(X)}.
$$

For classification, the common denominator $P(X)$ does not need to be computed explicitly. We compare

$$
P(C\mid X)\propto P(X\mid C)P(C).
$$

The components are:

- $P(C)$: prior probability of the class;
- $P(X\mid C)$: likelihood of the observed predictors under the class;
- $P(C\mid X)$: posterior probability after observing the predictors.

## The naive conditional-independence assumption

For predictors $X_1,\ldots,X_p$, Naive Bayes assumes conditional independence given the class:

$$
P(X_1,\ldots,X_p\mid C)=\prod_{j=1}^{p}P(X_j\mid C).
$$

Therefore,

$$
P(C\mid X_1,\ldots,X_p)\propto P(C)\prod_{j=1}^{p}P(X_j\mid C).
$$

::: {.callout-tip title="Key idea"}
The model computes a class score by multiplying the prior by conditional likelihood contributions from the predictors, then assigns the observation to the class with the larger posterior score.
:::

## Zero probabilities and Laplace smoothing

If a categorical level never appears with a class in the training data, its estimated conditional probability may be zero. Multiplication then forces the entire class score to zero.

Laplace smoothing replaces raw frequencies with adjusted counts:

$$
\widehat{P}(X_j=x\mid C=c)=\frac{n_{x,c}+\alpha}{n_c+\alpha k},
$$

where $k$ is the number of categories and a common choice is $\alpha=1$.

## Gaussian Naive Bayes

For continuous predictors, a common variant assumes

$$
X_j\mid C=c\sim N(\mu_{jc},\sigma_{jc}^2).
$$

The mean and variance are estimated separately for each predictor within each class.

## Strengths and limitations

Naive Bayes is fast, simple, probabilistic, and often effective in high-dimensional problems. Its limitations include a strong independence assumption, sensitivity to unobserved levels without smoothing, possible probability miscalibration, and distributional assumptions for continuous variables.

::: {.callout-warning title="Predictive usefulness does not validate the independence assumption"}
A good classification score does not imply that the predictors are truly conditionally independent. The assumption is a modeling simplification and should be described as such.
:::

## ATUS route

The Spanish edition applies Naive Bayes to an ATUS sample using month, hour, day of week, accident type, and cause. A stratified train/test split is used, Laplace smoothing is enabled, and performance is summarized with accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, precision, and F1.

The learned class priors and conditional distributions can also be inspected directly, which makes Naive Bayes particularly useful as a didactic probabilistic baseline.

## Probability interpretation

The `type = "raw"` prediction output contains model-based posterior scores. These are conditional on the fitted assumptions and the empirical training distribution.

::: {.callout-important title="Posterior scores are model-dependent"}
Posterior values should not automatically be interpreted as perfectly calibrated real-world probabilities. Calibration must be checked separately, especially when the sample prevalence has been modified.
:::

## COVID-19 educational route

The COVID-19 example uses the processed file selected by the reproducible preparation workflow rather than a hard-coded year.

```{r}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)

files_covid <- list.files(
  "../datos/covid19/procesados",
  pattern = "covid19_mexico_[0-9]{4}_ml_preparado\\.csv\\.gz$",
  full.names = TRUE
)

if (length(files_covid) == 0) {
  stop("No prepared COVID-19 data file was found.")
}

covid_nb <- read_csv(files_covid[1], show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  select(
    MURIO, EDAD, NEUMONIA, DIABETES, HIPERTENSION,
    OBESIDAD, RENAL_CRONICA, NUM_COMORBILIDADES
  ) |>
  drop_na()
```

For a teaching exercise, the outcome can be converted to a factor and the data split into training and test sets. The model can then combine Gaussian treatment of age with categorical or binary predictors.

::: {.callout-warning title="Educational use only"}
The resulting posterior scores describe the fitted educational dataset and must not be used for diagnosis, prognosis, or medical decisions.
:::

## Comparison with other classifiers

Naive Bayes differs from logistic regression because it models class-conditional predictor distributions rather than directly modeling the log-odds. Unlike k-NN and SVM, it does not rely on a distance-based decision rule. Unlike trees and Random Forest, it uses an explicit probabilistic decomposition.

## Chapter summary

Naive Bayes provides a transparent probabilistic classifier based on Bayes' theorem and a simplifying conditional-independence assumption. It is valuable as a fast baseline, but its probabilities and assumptions must be interpreted carefully and evaluated on data not used for training.
